render_attempts.prompt_text: Paint a monumental HUMAN-LED narrative WALL FRESCO, not an architectural visualization. The first thing the viewer sees is a large senior keeper and apprentice at the center, jointly comparing preserved knowledge while witnesses gather around them. This central human or human-led group occupies roughly one quarter of the composition and has expressive faces and gestures. Around it place about 18 additional human figures in at least 5 distinct groups. Show four clearly readable secondary episodes: scribes compare two damaged records in a side alcove; a family teaches a child from a preserved manuscript; couriers exchange custody beneath a bridge; restorers repair a fragile archive chamber. Use three unmistakable painted narrative registers: a symbolic celestial upper register, a crowded human middle register, and an intimate lower register of everyday human action; foreground, middle distance and far background are all inhabited. Architecture supports the people only: use arches, stairs, bridges, galleries, libraries, workshops, towers or ruins as inhabited stage scenery, never as the dominant subject, never as a single empty facade, portico, colonnade, hall or temple exterior. The image is visibly a wall fresco: surround the painted scene with an ornate but weathered fresco border, carved medallions, painted corner ornaments and cracked plaster edges; the border must frame the story rather than become an empty architectural facade. Paint it as a museum-scale monumental allegorical wall fresco, old-master figure painting, Renaissance and neoclassical grandeur, antique engraving-level detail, visibly painted on weathered lime plaster, cracked pigment, worn gilding, deep ultramarine, old gold, ivory stone, ochre, sepia and restrained crimson. Dense micro-scenes, layered human reactions, natural anatomy, coherent perspective, deep blue and old gold accents, worn mineral pigment, cracked plaster and intricate old-master line detail.

scene_plan.central_action: the mechanism visibly executes the ordered system process described by the source
supporting_actions: small side panels show earlier and later machine states
failed or unresolved states remain closed and visually subdued
style: painted directly on cracked aged lime plaster
ancient narrative fresco using mineral pigments
weathered hand-painted wall surface, not sculpture and not 3d render
layered historical storytelling with small side-register scenes
composition_rules: the scene archetype determines whether people are present
system names and internal identifiers never become humans or deities by name alone
named gates adapters protocols repositories and state-machine states remain mechanisms or provenance
the central visual action must come from the semantic role of the source, not from token name collisions
architecture may dominate only for ARCHITECTURAL_EVENT
all epistemic limits remain visually non-triumphal

The Washington, DC July 1952 wave produced multiple visual and radar reports and is documented by NARA as a major historical reporting episode.
Moses Lake: silver wingless object; witnesses were two Atomic Energy Commission employees.
George AFB: five flat-white discs in formation, making a near-90-degree turn and darting motions.

A secondary Blue Book archival summary explicitly notes the sighting occurred about an hour after an atomic-test cloud was visible in the direction of Las Vegas. This is temporally interesting but does not establish causal linkage.
Rapid City: at least five long silver objects in a box formation.
Walla Walla: oval object observed by an ex-military pilot.
Soap Lake: three glimmering objects observed for about ten minutes.
The Lubbock report is an exact nuclear-day STARLIKE_WITNESS morphology candidate.
Lubbock: eight yellow circular objects described as like large stars; first two in trail formation, others singly.
Offutt AFB: bright red object stationary for several minutes before rapidly departing.
1952 provides both clustered nuclear-test dates and a major non-nuclear human-report wave, making it a strong specificity stress test.
The available open evidence supports a substantial non-nuclear baseline in both photographic candidates and human reports. Nuclear-date proximity is therefore not a specific discriminator by itself.
The retrospective human-report layer does not show a positive relationship between monthly nuclear activity and monthly report counts.
Star-like human reports clearly occur both on nuclear dates and on non-nuclear dates, including the large July 1952 non-nuclear reporting wave.

The independent public POSS-I cohort did not reproduce a positive +/-1-day nuclear enhancement or a positive day+1 enhancement.
Only a rate difference that survives source, season, media-wave, duplicate-event, astronomy and reporting-opportunity controls may be called a human-report temporal association.
Multiple witnesses to one event are clustered as one event with witness_count rather than counted as independent events.
Same year and season/month with identical source inclusion rules, excluding nuclear windows, while explicitly controlling 1952 media/reporting-wave intensity.
Individual-sighting Blue Book index/case dates from the public T1206 finding aid or equivalent NARA-derived case index

The compact NARA public package is series-level material, not the individual-sighting date index. It contains 8 members (6 JPG and 2 PDF). Recursive metadata date extraction produced only 1951-05-21 and 1951-12-31 within the study interval, and inspection shows these are organization establishment/abolition dates, not sighting occurrence dates.
This prevents a subtle provenance error in which archival administrative dates could be accidentally joined to the nuclear calendar and interpreted as human sighting dates.
A Blue Book entry proves that an observation report entered the investigation system, not that its cause was extraordinary, extraterrestrial or non-human.
US National Archives / Project Blue Book

Project Blue Book case files are chronologically arranged and NARA states that a finding aid/index exists by sighting date and location. Most historical reports were collected with standardized Air Force questionnaires recording date, hour and observational description.

Record the first source-stratified human-witness control for the POSS-I/nuclear-date hypothesis, explicitly comparing reports near nuclear activity with reports on dates lacking nuclear tests and preventing star-like morphology from being treated as nuclear-specific by construction.
Retrospective sensitivity only. Historical NUFORC submissions have strong reporting-delay, memory, media and survivorship biases and cannot substitute for the contemporary Blue Book layer.
